feedback: If you predicted exactly one triangle and found two, that is the key surprise — the identical SSA data gave two genuinely different triangles. This is why SSA is called the ambiguous case.

If the compass arc crossed the 40° angle's other ray at two points, each crossing completes a valid but different triangle; if it just touches that ray at a single point there is one triangle (the tangent / right-angle case); if it crosses the ray at only one point because the other crossing falls behind the corner (this happens when the swinging side is at least as long as the base), there is also one triangle; if the arc never reaches that ray there is none.

When you fixed the angle BETWEEN the two sides (SAS), the third vertex was forced to a single location — the swing collapsed to one locked triangle. Notice you changed only where the angle sits, not the lengths.

If you justified 'one triangle' by naming SAS or 'two sides and an angle are given', check whether the angle is actually between the two named sides. Here it was opposite the 6 cm side, so SAS does not apply.
activities.intendedInsight: Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT determine a unique triangle — the free side can swing to meet the other arm of the angle in up to two places. When the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides (SAS), the triangle is locked. 'Included' is the word that matters.
learnerActions: Set up a fixed 9 cm base line. At one end, mark a 40° angle, drawing the second arm of that angle as a long ray rising from the corner. Pin a 6 cm 'arm' at the FAR end of the base (so the 40° angle sits OPPOSITE the 6 cm side, not between the two sides).
BEFORE moving anything, predict in writing: how many triangles can you complete, and WHY?

Swing the 6 cm arm (physically, or draw a compass arc of radius 6 cm centred at the far end of the base) and mark every point where the arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle (the ray rising from the angled corner) — each crossing is a possible third vertex.
Count the crossing points and draw each complete triangle you find.

Reconfigure with the40-degree angle between the6cm and9cm sides. Fix both sides on the two rays and join their free endpoints; compare this lockedSAS construction with the freeSSA arc. Rotated or reflected copies are still congruent, not different-sized solutions.
State in your own words why moving the angle from 'opposite' to 'between' changes the number of triangles.
activities.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles

feedback: For AAA you should have been able to build two triangles with identical angles but different sizes — equal angles fix the shape, not the size, so they are similar, not necessarily congruent.
For AAS, once two angles are known the third is forced (angles sum to 180°), so AAS carries the same information as ASA and fixes a unique triangle.

If every attempt 'worked' as a single triangle, revisit SSA and AAA carefully — valid AAA data always allow different sizes, and SSA data may give zero, one or two triangles depending on the measurements, so check whether a second triangle was possible.
Compare your outcome table with the construction you actually drew; a mismatch usually means a measurement was placed in the wrong position (e.g. the angle not truly between the two sides).
activities.intendedInsight: CompatibleSSS,SAS,ASA,AAS orRHS data determine a triangle up to congruence. Invalid measurements may determine none;SSA can allow zero,one or two, and validAAA data allow different sizes with the same shape. Reflected or rotated copies count as congruent, not new non-congruent triangles.
learnerActions: Using ruler, protractor and compass (or a dynamic geometry tool), attempt to construct a triangle from each data set: SSS (three given sides), SAS (two sides with the angle between them), ASA (two angles with the side between them), SSA (two sides with an angle opposite one), and AAA (three given angles).
For each, record whether you got exactly one triangle, more than one, or none.
For AAA, construct a second triangle with the same three angles but longer sides; compare it to the first.
Fill in a one/none/many outcome table listing each data set and its result.
Explain for AAS why giving two angles and one side forces a unique triangle even though you were not told the third angle directly.
activities.title: Construct from conditions: when do data fix a triangle?

feedback: If you wrote the vertices in an order that pairs a long side with a short one, the statement is wrong even if the triangles are congruent — reorder so matching parts line up.
Mark corresponding parts (ticks and arcs) before writing letters; this prevents reading off the wrong equal pairs.
A correct statement lets you list all three equal side pairs and all three equal angle pairs purely from the letters, with no diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of letters in a congruence statement encodes the correspondence: matching positions name matching vertices, sides and angles. The statement is only correct when every paired position is a genuinely equal part.
learnerActions: Given a pair of triangles with matched tick-marks on equal sides and arcs on equal angles, identify which vertex matches which.
Write the congruence statement in the form △ABC ≅ △___ so that the letter order pairs matching vertices.
From your statement, read off which sides are equal and which angles are equal, without looking back at the diagram.
Check: does the position of each letter in the two names point to a genuinely matching part? Mark the corresponding parts first, then write the statement.
Given a WRONG statement whose letters pair non-matching parts, correct it and explain what went wrong.
activities.title: Correspondence notation: △ABC ≅ △DEF

feedback: For validSAS data, the included angle fixes a unique triangle up to congruence. ForSSA, inspect the actual measurements: there can be zero,one or two triangles, so a single solution is possible. The9cm/6cm/40-degree example has two; do not generalise that count to everySSA case. RHS is a valid special right-triangle criterion.
'Same angles so congruent' is a similarity-vs-congruence error: equal angles fix shape only, so the triangles may be different sizes.
Reasoning that merely names a criterion without saying why the data force (or fail to force) a unique triangle is incomplete — the justification is the point.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which criterion applies and whether a data set fixes a unique triangle requires checking the included/non-included distinction and separating congruence from similarity — not pattern-matching 'two sides and an angle = SAS'.
learnerActions: For each given data set, answer: which criterion applies (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) — or none — and does it produce one triangle, none, or more than one?
When shown 'two sides and an angle', state explicitly whether the angle is between the two sides (SAS) or opposite one of them (SSA) before deciding.
When shown three equal angles, decide whether the triangles must be congruent, and justify.
Match corresponding parts in a △ABC ≅ △DEF item.
For each answer, write one sentence of reasoning that names WHY the data do or do not fix a unique triangle.
activities.title: Classify and reason: one, none or many?

feedback: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; check that the5cm length isBC, not a second leg.
Only one intersection lies on the chosen ray. A mirror image acrossAB is congruent, so it is not a second non-congruent solution.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side determine a right triangle up to congruence: this isRHS, not arbitrarySSA.
learnerActions: DrawAB=3cm and a perpendicular ray fromA; the angle atA is90degrees.
Draw a circle centred atB with radius5cm. Its intersection with the chosen perpendicular ray locatesC, soBC is the5cm hypotenuse andAB is the3cm side.
Compare two constructions with the same data and explain why they are congruent, including reflected or rotated copies.
activities.title: Construct a right triangle from hypotenuse and one side
